Furthermore, we outline the sensitivities of Super-Kamiokande to monopole fluxes for these three proton decay channels.

The rapid ionization of a sizable molecule can trigger a correlation-driven phenomenon known as charge migration, characterized by swift alterations in the distribution of electron density. Detecting this redistribution within few-femtosecond to attosecond intervals would constitute a real-time observation of electron correlation within the molecule; however, experimental proof of such a process had eluded researchers until now. This study presents a time-resolved analysis of charge migration in adenine, a biologically significant molecule, following ionization by an attosecond pulse with energies between 15-35 eV. We demonstrate that the formation of intact doubly charged adenine—achieved through a delayed, laser-induced second ionization event—serves as the hallmark of a charge localization mechanism driven by many-body excitations. This conclusion is corroborated by first-principles time-dependent simulations. These results provide promising avenues for managing molecular reactivity at the electronic timescale.

When the coupling-constant metamorphosis is employed with modified extended Hamiltonians, sufficient conditions have been established to ensure that the high-degree first integral of the transformed Hamiltonian is computed via the same procedure as the first integral of the original extended Hamiltonian. Illustrative cases include the Post-Winternitz system and the two-dimensional caged anisotropic oscillator.

The simplicity of supergravity $ \alpha$-attractor inflation models stems from Volkov-Akulov fermions, frequently realized within nilpotent superfields. This work investigates whether double-copy techniques can generate Dirac-Born-Infeld-Volkov-Akulov (DBIVA) theories coupled to supergravity. While color-dual bootstrap methods derive scattering amplitudes for pions and vectors up to the five-point tree level (order by order in mass-dimension), they necessitate a $tr(F^3)$ operator. Recent findings indicate that gauge theories containing this operator demand an infinite series of higher-derivative operators to satisfy color-kinematics duality. Consequently, the most conservative adjoint double-copy construction appears to necessitate the ultraviolet completion of DBIVA interactions with pure Poincaré supergravity into a family of theories where DBIVA-like particles couple to Weyl-Einstein supergravity. Additionally, we highlight an alternative approach for color-dual gauged pions that permits adjoint double-copy without higher-derivative towers, albeit by sacrificing exchange symmetry among scalars.

Building upon the standalone codes BIRMESC and ECLOUD (also known as PyECLOUD), we are creating a new, unified simulation framework designed to model how charged particle beams and microwaves interact within an electron cloud. Potential use cases include investigating microwave signal degradation in telecommunication satellites caused by electron clouds; analyzing microwave transmission methods employed in particle accelerators for cloud diagnostics; understanding microwave emission from electron clouds under magnetic fields; and exploring how injecting microwaves at specific frequencies and amplitudes could suppress electron cloud formation in accelerators. Several early simulation outcomes are included.

"Our team is proposing a comprehensive, full-scale energy demand response experiment within an office building. While this ambitious project promises significant community value, gathering training data for our reinforcement learning agent is both expensive and inherently restricted. Consequently, this work investigates how offline training can reduce both data acquisition and implementation expenses by accelerating convergence. We introduce two distinct strategies: first, pretraining our model on simulated tasks to provide a warm start, and second, employing a planning model trained to simulate the real-world rewards the agent receives. The results demonstrate the efficacy of offline reinforcement learning for enhancing price-setting efficiency in energy demand response applications."

This article outlines the technical specifications and features of the magnetic shield designed for 20-inch PMTs within the low-background OSIRIS facility. Constructing the shield utilizes a highly permeable amorphous alloy ribbon, enabling highly effective screening against the Earth's magnetic field with minimal material usage. Since material mass is critical for maintaining low radioactivity in such facilities, the employment of amorphous materials offers a cost-effective alternative to other magnetic shielding methods.

Prostate cancer (PCa) ranks among the most widespread and aggressive malignancies globally. The Gleason score (GS) system currently serves as the standard for classifying PCa and offers the most dependable approach for determining both severity and treatment protocols. In this traditional process, pathologists evaluate the spatial arrangement of cancer cells within the prostate tissue to assign a score ranging from 6 to 10. However, the conventional application of automatic analysis to prostate whole-slide images (WSIs) typically treats the task as a binary classification problem, thereby overlooking the nuanced distinctions provided by Gleason stages. To address this limitation, the current study introduces a probabilistic deep learning framework for ordinal classification capable of estimating the Gleason score directly from prostate WSIs. By framing the challenge as an ordinal regression problem using a differentiable probabilistic model, the research achieves both enhanced interpretability of results and superior accuracy compared to traditional deep classification and regression architectures.

This research investigates phase equilibria in a fluid confined within an open capillary slit created by positioning a finite-length wall (height $H$) a distance $L$ from a larger macroscopic surface. The rich behavior observed stems from the balance between two distinct capillary condensation mechanisms: meniscus depinning and corner filling, which vary according to the aspect ratio, $a=L/H$. In long capillaries where $a<2/\pi$, Type I condensation dominates; here, menisci remain pinned to the upper edges, exhibiting a specific edge contact angle. For intermediate capillaries with $2/\pi<a<1$, the transition type depends on the contact angle, ranging from pinned Type I condensates to unpinned Type II condensates where menisci overflow the reservoir. In short capillaries defined by $a>1$, Type II condensation consistently occurs. Across all regimes, large contact angles fully inhibit capillary condensation. Furthermore, we identify an additional continuous phase transition within the liquid-rich phase, linked to the rounding and subsequent depinning of menisci over the slit's open edges. We developed finite-size scaling models for these transitions and the connecting phase boundaries, integrating them with fluctuation theories for wetting and filling phenomena. Finally, our predictions were validated using comprehensive microscopic Density Functional Theory simulations, providing molecular-level insight into both condensation types and their suppression.

Even though large pre-trained code models have achieved remarkable advances across numerous code processing tasks, their widespread and fluent integration into software developers' daily routines is hindered by substantial resource demands. Specifically, these bulky models require hundreds of megabytes of memory and execute slowly on personal devices, leading to deployment challenges and a severely compromised user experience. To address this, we introduce Compressor, an innovative method capable of compressing pre-trained code models into extremely compact versions with negligible performance loss. Compressor approaches the design of tiny models by structurally simplifying the original pre-trained architecture through a search for a significantly reduced model that maintains architectural similarity. The method employs a genetic algorithm (GA) to guide this simplification. Leveraging the established insight that computational cost correlates with model capability, the GA strategy aims to maximize the model's Giga floating-point operations (GFLOPs)—a metric of computational intensity—while adhering to a strict target size constraint. Subsequently, the small model is trained using knowledge distillation, where unlabelled data generates outputs from the large model to serve as soft labels for training the smaller counterpart. We evaluate Compressor on two cutting-edge pre-trained models, CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT, applying them to critical tasks such as vulnerability prediction and clone detection. Using Compressor, we successfully reduced model sizes to approximately 3 MB, a reduction of 160 times compared to the originals. The evaluation shows that the compressed CodeBERT and GraphCodeBERT models achieve inference speeds 4.31$\times$ and 4.15$\times$ faster than their respective originals. More importantly, ...

The study proposes an unusual double-ray phenomenon of resonant light scattering in a periodic metasurface designed to generate robust non-specular reflection. This metasurface consists of silicon nanodisk arrays positioned atop a thin silica-on-metal substrate. Numerical simulations of light scattering demonstrate low-loss non-specular resonant reflection across all angles of incidence and for any polarization. The requirements for establishing an autocollimation scheme and detecting a non-specular ray that lies outside the plane of incidence are determined. Furthermore, adjusting the dielectric substrate's thickness is shown to regulate the bandwidth of non-specular reflection. Both the intensity of the specular and non-specular reflected rays can be manipulated by modifying the angle of incidence or the incident wave's polarization.

This work introduces novel differential privacy frameworks specifically designed for data products subject to simultaneous \emph{invariant} and \emph{integer} constraints, a requirement common in real-world private data curation tasks such as the 2020 U.S. Decennial Census. These dual constraints significantly hinder the creation of statistically useful, provably private outputs. To address this, we introduce \emph{integer subspace differential privacy}, formally defining privacy guarantees when both characteristics are maintained, and establish properties regarding its composition and post-processing capabilities. To facilitate sampling within potentially intricate discrete domains defined by these constraints, we develop two unbiased additive mechanisms—generalized Laplace and generalized Gaussian—by solving the associated Diophantine equations. Both mechanisms offer superior accuracy, characterized by error distributions featuring sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian tail probabilities, respectively. For practical implementation, we created a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, validating its empirical convergence using estimated upper bounds on total variation distance derived from $L$-lag coupling. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through three application scenarios: a synthetic problem involving intersecting invariants, a sensitive contingency table with fixed margins, and a 2010 Census county-level dataset requiring mandatory fixed state population totals.

Categories such as plants or furniture are acquired in early childhood and are essential for processing, organizing, and sharing knowledge about the world. Found across all cultures, these categories enable efficient representation of worldly complexity and display high consensus regarding their nature, underscoring a shared mental representation. However, models of category learning and representation have typically been evaluated using small-scale experiments that feature limited conceptual sets with artificially constrained traits, and their participants mostly consist of individuals from specific cultural and socio-economic backgrounds, frequently Western English speakers like U.S. college students. This research investigates if categorization models generalize when applied (a) to vast, noisy datasets mirroring real-world human environments, and (b) across different languages and cultures. We introduce a Bayesian cognitive model capable of simultaneously learning categories and their structured representations from natural language text, enabling (a) performance evaluation at a large scale and (b) application across a diverse linguistic spectrum. Our findings demonstrate that meaningful categories encompassing hundreds of concepts, alongside complex featural structures, emerge universally across languages. This study highlights the potential of integrating recent computational modeling advancements with large-scale naturalistic datasets in cognitive science.

In condensed-matter physics, electronic Mott insulators have been a significant area of study because of their complex connection to high-temperature superconductivity. However, unlike atomic systems where Mott phases have been recently demonstrated for both fermions and bosons, experimental evidence of an Mott insulator state using bosons in solid-state environments has remained elusive until now. In this study, we identify this signature by utilizing a Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian applied to semiconductor excitons trapped within two-dimensional lattices. Our focus is on the regime where on-site interaction energies are comparable to the energy differences between confined lattice states. We successfully observe accessible Mott phases featuring uniform filling of lattice sites by at most two excitons per site. Furthermore, our method allows for the on-demand programming of the lattice geometry confining the excitons. This technological flexibility, when paired with the long-range dipolar interactions inherent to excitons, opens a novel pathway to investigate many-body phases that spontaneously break lattice symmetry.

This study examines exclusive $\pi^-\Delta^{++}$ electroproduction using the handbag framework, where helicity amplitudes decompose into hard subprocesses and generalized parton distributions (GPDs). We establish the $p\text{-}\Delta$ transversity GPDs, sourcing non-flip helicity GPDs from established literature. For numerical predictions, we apply large-$N_C$ constraints to link specific $p\text{-}\Delta$ GPDs to $pp$ analogs while ignoring remaining contributions. Our calculation of twist-2 and twist-3 subprocess amplitudes incorporates quark transverse momentum alongside Sudakov suppression factors, leading to partial cross-section predictions for $\gamma^*p \to \pi^-\Delta^{++}$ within the large-$N_C$ regime.

Quantum walks serve as potent instruments for constructing search and sampling algorithms, specifically for generating quantum stationary states. However, the success probabilities of these methods typically fall significantly short of 1. While amplitude amplification can boost success rates, it introduces the "soufflé" problem; the optimal number of steps is critical. Ceasing execution before or after this optimal point can either limit success or diminish probability, creating practical challenges for implementations where the ideal step count is unknown. This study introduces generalized interpolated quantum walks, designed to enhance the success probability of search algorithms while simultaneously circumventing the soufflé problem. Furthermore, by integrating generalized interpolated quantum walks with quantum fast-forwarding, we reduce the number of walk operator calls from $\Theta((\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ to $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})\sqrt{\Heg})$ and decrease the required ancilla qubits from $\Theta(\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$ to $\Theta(\log\log(\varepsilon^{-1})+\log\sqrt{\Heg})$. In doing so, the algorithm maintains high success probability without suffering from the souffle issue, where $\varepsilon$ represents precision and $\Heg$ denotes the classical hitting time. Additionally, we demonstrate the utility of generalized interpolated quantum walks in improving the construction of quantum states representing stationary distributions. Finally, we present an application utilizing generalized interpolated quantum walks to build a slowly evolving Markov chain sequence, a requisite foundation for preparing adiabatic stationary states.

This work employs the functional renormalization group to analyze a $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric gauge theory featuring a quiral superfield coupled to a vector $U(1)$ superfield. We establish that the nonrenormalization theorem remains valid at the leading order of the supercovariant derivative expansion. Additionally, we calculate the beta functions and investigate fixed point behavior under local potential approximations, with a discussion of the regulators used.

The lattice size $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$ of a lattice polytope $P$ serves as a crucial invariant; originally defined in the context of bounding the total degree and bi-degree of equations for algebraic curves, the concept has long been present implicitly within geometric combinatorics. This paper demonstrates that for any empty lattice polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ and another class of lattice polytopes $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ with lattice width one, there exists a reduced basis of $\mathbb{Z}^3$ capable of calculating $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$. This finding enables a rapid algorithm for determining $\operatorname{ls_\Delta}(P)$ in these specific cases. Furthermore, we present a counterexample showing that a similar approach does not apply to arbitrary lattice polytopes $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ possessing a lattice width of one.

In 2017, Colorado implemented Risk-Limiting Audits (RLAs) throughout the state, utilizing both ballot-level comparison and ballot-polling techniques; however, these efforts were limited to contests within single counties because existing methods lacked the capability to efficiently audit cross-county races or combine these two audit types effectively. The current RLATool software requires enhancement to handle cross-county contests and improve efficiency in auditing small races. This paper addresses those gaps by outlining simple but inefficient approaches, more efficient stratified sampling techniques that merge ballot polling and comparison audits, and methods that integrate ballot-level comparisons with variable-size batch comparisons without relying on stratified sampling. The document concludes with recommendations supported by examples comparing these methods to current practices. Additionally, open-source code and interactive Jupyter notebooks are provided to implement these methods and facilitate further study.

Recent advancements in self-supervision have discovered feature representations comparable to those achieved with full supervision, offering benefits such as enhanced model robustness and improved out-of-distribution detection. In this paper, we present an empirical analysis to investigate how self-supervision—whether used for pre-training or integrated into adversarial training—influences a model's resilience against $l_2$ and $l_{\infty}$ perturbations and natural image corruptions. While self-supervision generally aids robustness, the outcome hinges heavily on specific implementation details. Merely adding self-supervision losses alongside standard adversarial training yields accuracy gains only for attack strengths ($\epsilon_{test}$) at or below the training budget ($\epsilon_{train}$); however, when $\epsilon_{test} \ge \epsilon_{train}$, model accuracy decreases. notably, increasing the loss weight regarding supervision exacerbates this performance degradation. We examined different strategies for blending self-supervision with adversarial training and found that using self-supervised objectives to jointly optimize network parameters and generate adversarial examples produces the most significant robustness improvements, effectively acting as ensemble adversarial training. Although pre-training with self-supervision outperforms random initialization for robust adversarial training, embedding self-supervision directly into the adversarial training process yields no measurable benefits in terms of robustness or accuracy.

This note follows Shu-Xue-Yao's prior work on enhanced groups and related $A$-type dualities \cite{BYY}, extending the investigation to classical groups of type $B$, $C$, and $D$. By first defining an enhanced Brauer algebra, we demonstrate restricted and Levi dualities via Proposition \ref{B dual}, which in turn provides a natural description of parabolic duality. Furthermore, Section \ref{3} details these relationships through explicit calculations in a specific scenario.

Bayesian optimization typically requires "inner optimization" of a non-convex, highly multi-modal acquisition function that often fails local numerical optimizers due to non-differentiability or other complexities. In these scenarios, it is standard practice to substitute continuous searches with discrete evaluations of random candidates. This work proposes an alternative where candidates are derived from a Delaunay triangulation of the current design set. We describe the generation of these "tricands," provide empirical evidence that they surpass both numerically optimized acquisitions and random candidate methods in synthetic and real-world simulations, and show their effectiveness within hybrid frameworks.

Recent years have highlighted quantum control techniques for three-level systems as a prominent area of inquiry within quantum information science and technology. This work introduces numerical simulations employing realistic experimental parameters to analyze quantum process tomography in the context of STIRAP (stimulated Raman adiabatic passage) and saSTIRAP (superadiabatic STIRAP). A fitting basis in the operator space is established, consisting of the identity operator alongside eight Gell-Mann operators, facilitating the computation of process matrices, each containing 81 elements ($9 \times 9$). The findings are examined for both the theoretical, decoherence-free scenario and a practically relevant situation that includes decoherence.

These results summarize the most recent ATLAS measurements of top-quark pair production accompanied by a photon, based on proton-proton collision data from the LHC at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The findings detail both inclusive and differential cross-section analyses conducted in single-lepton and dilepton final states, restricted to a fiducial volume that matches the detector's acceptance.

We report the detection of a novel cosmological signal, the Doppler-boosted Cosmic Infrared Background (DB-CIB), generated by the peculiar motions of the galaxies emitting the thermal dust observed in the cosmic infrared background. This new observable serves as an independent probe of the cosmic velocity field and is closely analogous to the established kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect. Notably, unlike the kSZ effect, DB-CIB is not subject to the 'kSZ optical depth degeneracy,' rendering it immune to complex galaxy formation processes. We anticipate that cross-correlating CCAT-Prime with DESI-like experiments will reveal this DB-CIB effect. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DB-CIB functions as a new CMB foreground that could introduce bias in future kSZ cross-correlation analyses if not adequately mitigated.

Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes (MMDP) serve as a robust framework for modeling sequential decision-making in cooperative multi-agent settings. Despite the development of various centralized and decentralized planning algorithms, the exponential expansion of state and joint action spaces, combined with dynamic environmental changes, hinders their ability to balance efficiency and scalability. While recent methods such as the centralized FV-MCTS-MP and the decentralized *Alternate maximization with Behavioural Cloning* (ABC) have shown significant promise, the former fails to adapt to dynamic environments and the latter neglects the absence of communication among agents. To address these limitations, we propose SiCLOP, a simulation-based online planning algorithm designed for multi-agent cooperation. SiCLOP integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with Coordination Graphs (CG) and Graph Neural Networks (GCN) to learn cooperative strategies and deliver real-time MMDP solutions. Furthermore, the algorithm enhances scalability through efficient action space pruning. In contrast to FV-MCTS-MP and ABC, SiCLOP incorporates transfer learning, allowing agents trained in one setting to operate effectively in others. We provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence within multi-agent contexts and present extensive empirical evidence demonstrating that SiCLOP significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art online planning techniques.

We introduce the 1-100 GeV spectral energy distribution (SED) for 148 recently detected high-synchrotron-peaked blazars (HSPs) from the First Brazil-ICRANet Gamma-ray Blazar catalogue (1BIGB). Many of these sources are absent from prior Fermi-LAT catalogues, marking a significant expansion of the known gamma-ray blazar population with novel spectral properties. Selected due to their excess emission between 0.3 and 500 GeV, these objects are promising candidates for very-high-energy (VHE) emission that may be detectable by the upcoming Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA). Our analysis utilizes nine years of observation data from the Fermi-LAT PASS8 dataset. We provide updated power-law parameters for all sources by reviewing their full broadband 0.3-500 GeV fits originally presented in the 1BIGB study. We evaluate their significance for VHE studies with existing and future instrumentation by extrapolating the gamma-raySEDs to higher energies for a subsample, accounting for extragalactic background light absorption. By comparing these extrapolations against CTA sensitivity curves, we estimate their potential detectability, highlighting two specific sources, 1BIGB J224910.6-130002 and 1BIGB J194356.2+211821. All newly presented gamma-raySEDs are made openly accessible through the Brazilian Science Data Center (BSDC) service at CBPF in Rio de Janeiro.

"End user analysis"—defined as extracting physics results from reconstructed and simulated data—is the focus of this summary for the Computational Frontier topical group at Snowmass 2021. High-energy physics experiments generate systems that execute common simulation, reconstruction, and calibration processes, yielding shared data. These granular datasets are subsequently refined into diverse analysis samples, often targeted for specific physics goals through triggers or data object filtering. Researchers, or end users, then process these samples to derive physics outcomes. Community consensus has categorized the end user analysis landscape into five key domains: Analysis Ecosystems, Analysis Models, Dataset Bookkeeping and Formats, Collaborative Software, and Training. The following findings and recommendations address how these critical areas influence end user analysis.

We have demonstrated that, for smooth projective families of varieties with a good minimal model where the base dimension is five or less and its Kodaira dimension is non-negative, the variation serves as a lower bound for the base's Kodaira dimension. This result confirms the Kebekus-Kovacs conjecture for all such base spaces of dimension at most five.
